candidates.title: Successful rechallenge with almonertinib and corticosteroids after gefitinib-induced interstitial lung disease: A case report and literature review.
candidates.abstract:
RATIONALE: First-generation epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) are highly effective in EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC); however, drug-induced interstitial lung disease (ILD) remains a rare but potentially fatal adverse event. The safety and efficacy of EGFR-TKI rechallenge - either with the same agent or an alternative one - following ILD resolution are not established and represent a significant clinical knowledge gap.
PATIENT CONCERNS: A 53-year-old never-smoking woman with stage IV lung adenocarcinoma - detected to harbor an L858R mutation in exon 21 of the EGFR gene - developed progressive dyspnea and hypoxemia after 2 months of first-line gefitinib therapy, despite confirmed initial radiographic and clinical response.
DIAGNOSES: The patient was diagnosed with grade 3 gefitinib-associated ILD.
INTERVENTIONS: With the discontinuation of gefitinib, the patient was given methylprednisolone to resolve ILD. To control advanced lung adenocarcinoma progression, the patient was subjected to 6 cycles of treatment using pemetrexed, carboplatin, and bevacizumab, with measurable tumor shrinkage, followed by maintenance therapy with bevacizumab. Furthermore, given the tumor progression 14 months later, the patient was prescribed docetaxel plus bevacizumab to restore control. Ten months later, the patient experienced disease progression and strongly requested to use EGFR-TKIs again given prior response to EGFR-TKI. The patient was rechallenged with almonertinib, a third-generation EGFR-TKI, and methylprednisolone.
OUTCOMES: The patient had measurable tumor shrinkage, with sustained tumor control and no recurrence of pulmonary toxicity. As of last follow-up, she maintained progression-free survival for approximately 8 months on almonertinib.

candidates.title: Radiation-induced Salivary Gland Fibrosis: Pathogenesis and Potential Targets for Therapeutic Intervention.
candidates.abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: This review focuses on radiotherapy (RT)-induced salivary gland (SG) fibrosis and current treatment options. Furthermore, we suggest that based on their mechanisms of action, three recently approved anti-fibrotic drugs (namely nintedanib, pirfenidone, and nerandomilast), could be repurposed to treat the fibrosis underlying RT-induced SG hypofunction.
RECENT FINDINGS: Although saliva substitutes and secretory stimulants are used clinically to relieve symptoms of xerostomia and reduce some of the consequences of hyposalivation, these approaches do not repair underlying damage to SGs due to cancer therapy. Consequently, treatment of salivary hypofunction and xerostomia induced by RT is a major, unmet medical need. The molecular processes underlying RT-induced SG injury culminate in inflammation and oxidative stress associated with SG fibrosis and resultant hyposalivation. Identification of these processes provides potential targets for mechanism-based interventions for treatment of this disorder.
candidates.fulltext: BackgroundXerostomia, commonly known as dry mouth, is a distressing condition characterized by a patient’s subjective sense of a reduced or absent saliva flow [1]. Xerostomia could be clinically accompanied by hyposalivation, also called salivary gland hypofunction [2]. It can result from various etiologies, including medications, radiation therapy, autoimmune disorders, and systemic conditions [3, 4]. This condition poses significant challenges to patients’ quality of life due to increased risk of mucositis, difficulties in speaking, painful swallowing, and predisposition to oral infections. In this review, we will explore the clinical insights of cancer treatment-related xerostomia, discuss its pathophysiology, evaluate the available treatment options and ongoing candidates, and provide future perspectives.Etiology and pathophysiologySaliva is pivotal in maintaining oral health by lubricating the oral mucosa, facilitating speech, bolus formation, digestion, and protection against dental caries and oral infections [5, 6]. Xerostomia disrupts this delicate balance, leading to a cascade of adverse effects. Three main salivary glands, parotid, submandibular, and sublingual, along with numerous minor salivary glands distributed throughout the oral cavity, carry the duty of saliva production. Under normal physiological conditions, saliva production is regulated by a complex interplay of neural, hormonal, and local factors, including autonomic nervous system innervation and stimulation by cholinergic and adrenergic neurotransmitters [7]. Various etiologies, such as medications, radiation therapy, autoimmune diseases, and systemic conditions, can disrupt salivary gland function, resulting in xerostomia [8].The pathophysiology of xerostomia involves dysfunction in salivary gland secretion, either due to reduced saliva production or altered saliva composition [9–13]:Reduced saliva production: Several factors could contribute to reduced saliva production, including:oRadiation therapy: As the leading cause of hyposalivation in cancer patients, radiation therapy to head, neck, and upper thoracic regions could irreversibly damage salivary gland tissues and impair their ability to produce saliva, leading to acute and chronic xerostomia.oMedications: Certain medications, including anticholinergics, antidepressants, antihypertensives, and antihistamines, can inhibit salivary gland secretion by blocking muscarinic receptors or interfering with neurotransmitter release.oSystemic diseases: Autoimmune disorders, such as Sjögren’s syndrome, and systemic conditions, such as diabetes mellitus, could cause immune-mediated destruction of salivary gland tissues, resulting in xerostomia.Altered saliva composition: In addition to reduced saliva production, xerostomia can also result from altered saliva composition, including changes in electrolyte concentrations, pH levels, and protein content. Reduced saliva flow rates can lead to increased salivary viscosity and decreased buffering capacity, predisposing individuals to dental caries and oral infections. Altered saliva composition also affects oral mucosal integrity.Several factors could affect the salivary glands and saliva composition, resulting in xerostomia. Table 1 summarizes the most important general causes of xerostomia. However, cancer treatment-related xerostomia could be classified to five main categories:Table 1Causes of xerostomiaEtiologyDescriptionRadiation therapy and radioisotopesRadionuclides and external radiation therapy involving the head and neck region could reversibly or irreversibly damage the salivary glandsSystemic cytotoxic chemotherapy/immunotherapyChemotherapeutic agents such as 5-Fluorouracil result in altered salivary gland functionsMedicationsAnticholinergics, antidepressants, antihypertensives, and antihistamines are common reasons for drug-induced xerostomiaUnderlying systemic diseaseSjögren’s syndrome, diabetes mellitus, and autoimmune diseases can manifest with xerostomiaDehydrationInadequate fluid intake or conditions causing dehydration can result in transient xerostomiaRadiation therapy-inducedXerostomia is one of the most common adverse effects of radiation therapy [14, 15]. The salivary glands, including the major parotid, submandibular, and sublingual glands, are often exposed to radiation during treatment, leading to long-term and irreversible damage to the glandular tissues and impairment of saliva production. Previous studies have suggested that around two-third of the patients undergoing conventional two-dimensional radiotherapy techniques experience moderate-to-severe degrees of xerostomia due to irreversible damage to salivary glands [16, 17]. Newer approaches, such as intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT), come with a reduced post-radiation xerostomia incidence and enhanced salivary recovery [18, 19]. candidates.title: Metallothionein-2A licenses an S100A8 alarmin program to drive epithelial-mesenchymal transition in pulmonary fibrosis.
candidates.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pulmonary fibrosis (PF) is a progressive interstitial lung disease driven in part by epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), but the upstream epithelial regulators remain undefined, and conventional screens rarely separate causal drivers from bystanders.
METHODS: We integrated interpretable machine learning (SHAP-interpreted LASSO across five transcriptomic cohorts), single-cell virtual gene knockout (VGKO), protein-protein docking with molecular dynamics, co-immunoprecipitation and surface plasmon resonance, a bleomycin mouse model, and loss-/gain-of-function studies in TGF-β1-stimulated BEAS-2B cells, complemented by AI-guided drug screening.
RESULTS: SHAP nominated MT2A as a positively weighted predictor broadly expressed across multiple cell subpopulations, and in silico knockout nominated S100A8 as its leading candidate downstream target, yielding a directional MT2A→S100A8 hypothesis. Docking and molecular dynamics predicted a stable MT2A-S100A8 complex, co-immunoprecipitation recovered both proteins from the same complex in cells, and surface plasmon resonance measured direct binding with an apparent dissociation constant of 88 ± 20 nM. MT2A and S100A8 were co-upregulated in fibrotic mouse lung. In epithelial cells, MT2A knockdown reduced S100A8 and reversed the EMT signature, whereas overexpression amplified it. Reciprocal epistasis placed S100A8 downstream of MT2A as its obligate effector: re-expressing S100A8 restored EMT in MT2A-depleted cells, and silencing S100A8 abolished the pro-fibrotic effect of MT2A overexpression. AI screening nominated BRD-K54403101 as a candidate MT2A binder.
CONCLUSION: We identify MT2A as broadly expressed across single-cell clusters and show that in bronchial epithelial cells MT2A sustains S100A8, which is necessary and sufficient to drive the EMT program. The experimentally defined MT2A-S100A8 axis is a tractable target in pulmonary fibrosis.
candidates.fulltext: 1IntroductionPulmonary fibrosis (PF), of which idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is the most aggressive form, is a chronic and progressive interstitial lung disease characterized by relentless scarring of the lung parenchyma, declining gas exchange and a median survival of three to five years after diagnosis (1, 2). Approved antifibrotic agents—pirfenidone (3, 4), nintedanib (5, 6), and the preferential phosphodiesterase-4B (PDE4B) inhibitor nerandomilast (7, 8)—modestly slow lung-function decline but neither halt nor reverse established fibrosis, and are frequently limited by toxicity and high discontinuation rates. Closing this therapeutic gap requires identifying the upstream regulators that convert a reparative response into pathological remodeling.The alveolar and airway epithelium is increasingly recognized as an initiating compartment in this process. Repetitive micro-injury provokes aberrant epithelial activation, impaired regeneration and acquisition of a pro-fibrotic secretory phenotype, in part through epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT), during which epithelial cells lose apical–basal polarity and cell–cell adhesion, downregulate E-cadherin (CDH1, E-cad), and gain mesenchymal markers including vimentin (VIM), fibronectin 1 (FN1) and type I collagen (COL1A1) (9). Identifying the molecular switches that initiate this epithelial program is therefore central to understanding fibrotic progression.A major obstacle is that conventional differential-expression screens rank genes by association but often cannot distinguish drivers from bystanders, nor specify the direction of causal influence. Recent computational advances address this limitation directly: interpretable machine learning quantifies and signs each feature’s contribution to a phenotype, while single-cell virtual gene knockout perturbs an inferred gene-regulatory network in silico to predict the transcriptional consequences of removing a candidate driver. Coupling these complementary approaches offers a principled route from correlation to a testable, direction-aware causal hypothesis.Applying this strategy to PF, our pipeline converged on two effectors that recur in fibrotic and inflammatory tissue but have not been mechanistically linked. Metallothionein-2A (MT2A) is a small, cysteine-rich, metal-binding protein implicated in zinc homeostasis, redox buffering and the modulation of inflammatory signaling, yet its role in lung fibrosis remains essentially uncharacterized (10, 11). S100A8, a calcium-binding alarmin, is a potent amplifier of innate-immune and chemotactic signaling and a recognized marker of inflammatory tissue states (12–14). We therefore hypothesized that MT2A acts upstream to sustain S100A8 expression, and that this directional MT2A-S100A8 axis drives epithelial EMT and thereby promotes fibrotic progression in PF.To test this hypothesis, interpretable machine learning across multiple cohorts nominated MT2A as a high-priority, positively weighted predictor; Single-cell profiling showed its robust expression across major immune lineages, and virtual knockout nominated S100A8 as its dominant downstream target. Given that MT2A is a broadly induced stress-response protein and S100A8 is induced in both myeloid and epithelial compartments during fibrosis, we tested the predicted MT2A-S100A8 axis in bronchial epithelial cells, where EMT originates. We then tested the predicted MT2A-S100A8 interaction structurally and biochemically, including by surface plasmon resonance, defined the hierarchy of the axis through loss-of-function, gain-of-function and reciprocal epistasis experiments in epithelial cells, confirmed co-regulation in vivo, and used AI-guided screening to prioritize a candidate MT2A-targeting small molecule. Raw data in MINiML format underwent a standardized preprocessing pipeline. Non-normalized data were taken log2 transformation, and quantile normalization was applied to ensure comparability across samples. Probe IDs were mapped to official gene symbols using the corresponding platform annotation files; probes matching multiple genes were excluded, and expression values for genes matched by multiple probes were averaged (17). candidates.title: Non-RA screening for systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases using a machine learning model based on physical findings and blood test data.
candidates.journal: BMC medical informatics and decision making
candidates.abstract:
BACKGROUND: In patients with systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases (SARDs), particularly patients with non-rheumatoid arthritis (non-RA), the incidence of severe conditions such as interstitial pneumonia and pulmonary arterial hypertension is high. Therefore, early referral of these patients to university hospitals or other institutions capable of comprehensive medical care is desirable. However, the substantial overlap in clinical presentations across SARDs makes differentiation challenging, and objective tools to support disease classification in routine clinical practice remain limited. In this study, a machine learning based classifier was developed to distinguish Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) from non‑RA conditions using general physical findings and routine blood test data, focusing on patients who were diagnosed with a predefined set of SARDs from a secondary‑care teaching hospital.
METHODS: An observational retrospective study was conducted on 571 patients initially diagnosed with SARDs. From the hospital's clinical information database, patients' diagnoses, blood test results, and physical findings were extracted from the hospital's clinical information database to create the dataset. Physical findings were extracted as structured data using natural language processing from medical records written in a free description format by the attending physicians. For patient classification, some non-RA screening model using three classification algorithms were developed: Naive Bayes, Linear Support Vector Machines, and Random Forest.
RESULTS: RA and non-RA diseases share common clinical symptoms, with joint symptoms observed in over 40% of patients with the target diseases. Of the screening models, the random forest model performed the best, achieving a sensitivity of 77.3% and a specificity of 72.5%.

candidates.title: Combining handcrafted radiomics features and deep learning features within different regions of interest in planning CT images for the prediction of symptomatic radiation pneumonitis in locally advanced non-small cell lung cancer.
candidates.abstract:
PURPOSE: To predict symptomatic radiation pneumonitis (RP) in locally advanced non-small cell lung cancer (LA-NSCLC) patients by handcrafted radiomics (HCR) and deep learning (DL) features of three different regions of interest (ROIs) in normal lung tissue.
METHODS: Ninety LA-NSCLC patients from Center A were collected as the development cohort, and an additional 57 patients from Center B were collected as the external validation set. Clinical data and lung dose-volume parameters were collected from the patients, and univariate analysis was conducted. Three ROIs in lung were delineated in pre-radiotherapy CT images: Lung-PTV, Lung-GTV, and PTV-GTV. For each ROI, 1046 HCR features and 512 DL features were respectively extracted, and then correlated. For each ROI, three models (HCR, DLR, and a hybrid model) were developed with feature selection via Spearman correlation, mRMR, the LASSO method, and SVM-based modeling. And finally, their performance was evaluated and compared using AUC values from ROC curves. The optimal model was selected by comparing the best AUC through internal validation results, and then external validation was conducted. Calibration and decision curve analyses were used to evaluate the model.
RESULTS: In the development cohort, univariate analysis revealed no statistically significant associations with RP. The correlation analysis revealed a weak correlation between HCR and DL features. In internal validation, for Lung-PTV, Lung-GTV and PTV-GTV, HCR models achieved AUCs of 0.658 (95%CI: 0.645-0.671), 0.659 (95%CI: 0.646-0.672), and 0.890 (95%CI: 0.881-0.899); DLR models obtained AUCs of 0.832 (95%CI: 0.824-0.840), 0.900 (95%CI: 0.893-0.907), and 0.777 (95%CI: 0.766-0.788); and the hybrid model showed AUCs of 0.838 (95%CI: 0.831-0.846), 0.901 (95%CI: 0.894-0.908), and 0.919 (95%CI: 0.912-0.926). candidates.fulltext: BackgroundRadiotherapy is used consistently throughout lung cancer treatment. Radiation pneumonitis (RP) is a common complication of thoracic radiotherapy. According to the relevant literature, the incidence rate of RP is approximately 30% [1]. RP occurs when normal lung tissue in the radiation field is affected by passing radiation, which causes alveolar exudation inflammation. It is typically marked by dyspnoea, dry cough, hypoxemia, and low fever. Pathological anatomy shows alveolar septal oedema, endothelial cell swelling, vascular wall thickening, and other changes [2, 3]. The main manifestations of CT are patchy and uniform flocculent blurred shadows in the radiological field, accompanied by thickened blood vessels and bronchial shadows and indistinct boundaries with surrounding normal lung tissue. The spots in the radiological area are solid, with a higher density than ground glass opacities, clear edges, and clear boundaries with normal tissue [4]. We attach CT images to demonstrate the above features (Fig. 1).Fig.1CT image of RP A: Axial image from a CT angiogram performed 5 months after radiotherapy demonstrating consolidation and atelectasis consistent with radiation pneumonitis and fibrosis. B: The image demonstrates airspace consolidation in the medial right middle lobe and superior right lower lobe with traction bronchiectasis and reticulation within the radiation field, consistent with evolution of radiation fibrosisThe interval between the onset of RP and radiotherapy varies in length. Acute RP usually occurs within a few days after irradiation, while most chronic RP occurs within the first 12 weeks to 6 months after radiotherapy [5]. Once RP occurs, it causes irreversible fibrous lesions and even fibrosis of the lung tissue, damages respiratory function, and seriously influences the quality of life and survival of patients.The risk factors were evaluated in the era of chemotherapy. Regimens such as gemcitabine, patients with diabetes, and the V20 of lung dose ≥ 30% have definite relationships with the occurrence of RP. To date, with the advent of immunotherapy, the risk factors for RP urgently need to be re-evaluated to avoid serious events and improve overall efficacy.Physical parameters of radiation therapyThe doses of the opposite mediastinumA previous retrospective analysis by Takayuki Mikimoto et al. showed that a radiation dose to the opposite mediastinum greater than 40 Gy could be a risk factor for severe RP [6]. The possible reason for this relationship is that an irradiation dose greater than 40 Gy may cause a larger radiation field that includes the contralateral mediastinum. Second, contralateral lymphatic outflow, which is more vulnerable to damage than normal lung tissue and more prone to inflammatory cell infiltration and tissue damage, may be damaged [6].DVHThe dose-volume histogram (DVH) parameters of radiotherapy mainly include the mean lung dose (MLD) and V5(Percentage of lung volume exposed to radiation greater than 5 Gy to total lung volume), V10(Percentage of lung volume exposed to radiation greater than 10 Gy to total lung volume), V20(Percentage of lung volume exposed to radiation greater than 20 Gy to total lung volume), V30(Percentage of lung volume exposed to radiation greater than 30 Gy to total lung volume) [7]. The occurrence and severity of RP are often closely related to the lung volume that exceeds the lung radiation tolerance threshold. When the entire lung is irradiated, the threshold of RP can be as low as 7 Gy, but when part of the lung is irradiated, the threshold of RP can be as high as 20–30 Gy [8]. In a univariate statistical analysis of RP during concurrent chemoradiotherapy conducted by Tsujino et al., all DVH parameters were related to the occurrence of ≥ grade 3 RP [7].V20In clinical radiotherapy for lung cancer, V20 is typically used as a parameter to evaluate the treatment plan. Many studies have reported that V20 can be invoked as an independent risk factor for RP. A retrospective analysis published by Graham MV et al. [9] confirmed V20 as a risk factor for RP. The results showed that the incidence of RP (above grade 2) was 0.7% and 36% two years later when V20 was less than 22% and more than 40%, respectively. At the same time, Tsujin [10], Leprieur [11], Pinnix [12], Farr [13], and other studies confirmed that the incidence of RP increased with increasing V20. Therefore, V20 is strictly limited in the synchronous chemoradiotherapy mode. A multivariate statistical analysis of RP during concurrent chemoradiotherapy conducted by Tsujino [7] showed that V20 ≥ 26% was a risk factor for RP of grade 3 or above. candidates.title: [Video-assisted Thoracic Surgery for an Enlarging Pneumatocele After with Hemorrhagic Contents After Severe Pneumonia].
candidates.journal: Kyobu geka. The Japanese journal of thoracic surgery
candidates.abstract: A 62-year-old man developed severe pneumonia complicated by acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) and was treated with mechanical ventilation and systemic steroids for organizing pneumonia. During treatment for organizing pneumonia, bilateral pneumatoceles and right pneumothorax were detected. Although the pneumothorax resolved after chest drainage, the right pneumatocele progres sively enlarged with increasing fluid components suspected to be hemorrhagic. Because percutaneous drainage was considered ineffective and surgical hemostasis might be necessary, video-assisted thoracic surgery was performed. The pneumatocele was opened, and intracavitary hematoma was removed. No air leakage from the base of pneumatocele was detected. The base of the lesion was treated with soft coagulation and covered with a polyglycolic acid sheet and fibrin glue. Histopathological examination revealed preserved visceral pleural elastic layers with subpleural alveolar structures, suggesting detach ment within the subpleural lung parenchyma. Accumulation of hematoma within the pneumatocele and microbleeding possibly enhanced by anticoagulation therapy might have contributed to its enlargement. Surgical intervention may be an effective treatment option for pneumatoceles accompanied by hemor rhagic contents and progressive enlargement.

candidates.title: [Current State of the Asbestos Outpatient Clinic and an Evaluation of Asbestos Bodies].
candidates.journal: Kyobu geka. The Japanese journal of thoracic surgery
candidates.abstract: A total of 46 cases visited our hospital's asbestos outpatient clinic over 12-year period from May 2013 to April 2025. The reasons for referral were as follows:15 cases were referred by the Labor Bureau, 15 by other departments within our hospital, 10 by other medical institutions, and six were self-referred. A history of asbestos exposure was identified in 40 cases (87%). Nine patients underwent surgery for asbestos-related malignancies (five primary lung cancers and four pleural mesotheliomas). In two lung cancer patients who underwent lobectomy, high concentrations of asbestos bodies were detected in non-cancerous lung tissue using a tissue digestion method, whereas none were identified by Berlin blue staining of routine sections. The diagnosis of asbestos-related lung cancer in general hospitals remains challenging.

candidates.title: [HER2-Positive Colorectal Cancer-from Diagnosis to Anti-HER2 Therapy].
candidates.journal: Gan to kagaku ryoho. Cancer & chemotherapy
candidates.abstract: HER2-positive colorectal cancer (CRC) represents a rare but clinically significant molecular subset, accounting for 2-4% of all CRCs. This subtype is enriched in left-sided and rectal tumors and in RAS/BRAF wild-type cases, and has been identified as an independent poor prognostic factor. Diagnosis relies on immunohistochemistry (IHC), fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), and next-generation sequencing (NGS)-based companion diagnostics. Trastuzumab plus pertuzumab (TRA + PER) is the established standard for RAS wild-type, HER2-positive CRC after prior standard chemotherapy (TRIUMPH: ORR 30%, median PFS 4.0 months). In March 2026, trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd) was approved in Japan for HER2-positive solid tumors including CRC (DESTINY-CRC02: 5.4 mg/kg cohort, ORR 38%, median PFS 5.8 months), even in RAS-mutant cases. Key adverse events include infusion reactions and cardiac dysfunction with TRA + PER, and interstitial lung disease (ILD; particularly high incidence in Japanese patients at 26%) and myelosuppression with T-DXd. Comprehensive HER2 testing prior to first-line therapy is recommended regardless of RAS/BRAF status. This review summarizes the epidemiology, diagnostic approach, efficacy data, and safety management of anti-HER2 therapy for HER2-positive CRC.

candidates.title: Genomic ascertainment refines the population prevalence and phenotype associations of germline TERT variants.
candidates.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Individuals with deleterious germline variants in telomerase (encoded by TERT) are at high risk of pulmonary fibrosis (PF), liver disease (LD), bone marrow failure, head/neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC), and other complications. Clinically ascertained cohorts are subject to biased ascertainment of affected individuals and families with early onset, complex disease. This study used genomic ascertainment to determine prevalence of deleterious TERT variants and the associated risks of telomere biology disorder (TBD) phenotypes.
METHODS: TERT variants were extracted from exome sequencing data in UK Biobank (UKB, 469,377 exomes) and Geisinger-Regeneron DiscovEHR collaboration (DiscovEHR, 170,503 exomes). Cases were individuals with heterozygous deleterious TERT variants classified per modified ACMG/AMP criteria. Controls excluded rare, exonic, and splice site TERT variants. Electronic health records were assessed for TBD-related ICD10 codes. Case-control comparisons were done separately for UKB and DiscovEHR, accounting for smoking, alcohol, BMI, sex, genetic ancestry, and birthyear.
RESULTS: There were 64 deleterious TERT variants in 203 UKB participants and 32 in 138 DiscovEHR participants. Prevalence estimates were 1:2,312 in UKB and 1:1,235 in DiscovEHR. Risk of PF was significantly increased for TERT heterozygotes compared with controls (UKB: odds ratio [OR] 10.9 95% confidence interval [CI]: 6.11-19.45, p < 0.001; DiscovEHR: OR 6.64, 95% CI: 3.31-13.3, p < 0.001). Deleterious TERT variants were also associated with higher risk of LD (OR 2.4, 95% CI:1.25-4.59, p = 0.038) and HNSCC (OR 5.75, 95% CI: 2.36-14.02, p = 0.001) in UKB but not in DiscovEHR.
CONCLUSIONS: Rare deleterious TERT variants were present in 0.04 to 0.08% of the populations studied. Genomic ascertainment shows a predominance of pulmonary phenotypes, with PF associated with deleterious TERT variants in both cohorts. candidates.fulltext: IntroductionTelomeres are long (TTAGGG)n nucleotide repeats and a protein complex at chromosome ends essential for genomic stability that shorten with each cell division due to the inability of DNA polymerase to fully replicate DNA ends [1]. Telomerase reverse transcriptase, encoded by TERT, extends telomeric nucleotide repeats in germ and stem cells, however TERT is repressed in differentiated cells. Germline pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants (P/LP) in TERT are associated with short telomeres, increased risk of pulmonary fibrosis (PF), bone marrow failure (BMF), cancer, and other complications [2–13].TERT is one of at least 15 telomere maintenance genes with rare germline P/LP variants associated with the telomere biology disorders (TBDs) [14–16]. Genotype-phenotype studies suggest that heterozygous TINF2, X-linked recessive (DKC1), or autosomal recessive (e.g. TERT, CTC1, PARN, RTEL1, WRAP53) P/LP variants are more likely to be associated with childhood onset TBDs, including dyskeratosis congenita [17]. Heterozygous P/LP variants in TERT, TERC, RTEL1, PARN, or ZCCHC8 are more likely to present in adulthood with isolated BMF, PF, liver disease, and/or cancer, and usually have an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern [18]. Notably, heterozygous P/LP TERT variants are present in 10–20% of PF families, making them one of the most common causes of familial PF [10,11,19,20].The age at onset of TERT-related manifestations can be highly variable, even within families, due to incomplete penetrance and variable expressivity [14,21]. To date, studies of TBDs have focused on clinically ascertained individuals and families and consequently are often biased towards severe and/or early-onset disease. The prevalence of TBDs due to P/LP TERT variants in the general population is currently unknown [22].Linking genomic databases with clinical data provides the opportunity to identify individuals with P/LP variants of interest and then objectively assess their associated phenotypes [23]. This genomic ascertainment or “genome-first” approach minimizes ascertainment bias caused by defining an inherited disorder by clinical manifestations and can provide estimates of population penetrance and variant-associated disease risk. This approach has been highly informative in phenotype characterization and quantification in cancer predisposition syndromes [24,25].This study is the first to determine the population prevalence of rare germline TERT variants and explore their TBD-associated phenotypes using data from the United Kingdom Biobank (UKB) and the Geisinger-Regeneron DiscovEHR collaboration (DiscovEHR) and provides key insights as to the public health impact of TERT-associated TBDs.MethodsEthical statementThis research was conducted using the UKB Resource under application #54389. This study used whole exome sequencing (WES) variant data from peripheral blood DNA available for research use in total of 469,377 individuals from the UKB linked electronic health records (EHR), cancer and death registries [27–29]. We used the UKB data released on July 12, 2024 [23,30] (UKB application number 54389). Participants withdrawn from the UKB study as of August 2025 were excluded from this analysis.DiscovEHR consists of 170,503 unselected participants (age 0–90 + years) recruited from in- and outpatient sites within the Geisinger, a large regional medical system headquartered in Danville, Pennsylvania (PA), USA, serving central and northeast PA [31,32]. Informed consent was obtained from DiscovEHR participants or their legal guardians to undergo WES and SNP array genotyping by Regeneron Genetics Center, Tarrytown, NY, USA and to have their health information linked to Geisinger for research purposes (protocol #2006–0258) [32]. candidates.title: Integrating proteomics to map immune landscape and protein biomarkers for risk stratification in childhood Langerhans cell histiocytosis.
candidates.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) is a rare pediatric disease with marked clinical heterogeneity. Current risk stratification relies on the extent of organ involvement and risk-organ status, yet reliable protein biomarkers for distinguishing LCH subtypes are lacking.
METHODS: We performed proteomic analysis on 56 formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) pediatric LCH tissue samples and 10 normal skin controls, quantifying 6, 914 proteins. Machine-learning approaches were integrated with weighted correlation network analysis for exploratory identification of candidate protein biomarkers and internal classification analysis. Candidate markers were validated by immunohistochemistry. The CIBERSORT deconvolution algorithm was employed to estimate the immune cell infiltration.
RESULTS: Proteomic profiling clearly distinguished LCH from controls. Functional protein modules and candidate protein biomarkers were identified across different LCH subtypes. Significant differences in immune cell infiltration were also observed, revealing enhanced innate immune activation and cytotoxic T cell responses in multisystem LCH compared with single-system LCH, as well as in LCH with risk-organ involvement versus those without. In exploratory internal classification analyses, the SVM model yielded an accuracy, AUC, and F1 score of 1.000 (95% CI: 1.000-1.000) for distinguishing multisystem from single-system LCH. For risk-organ involvement, the KNN model yielded an accuracy of 0.800 (95% CI: 0.500-1.000) and an AUC of 0.880 (95% CI: 0.600-1.000).
CONCLUSION: To our knowledge, this is the first large-scale FFPE-based proteomic study in pediatric LCH to reveal subtype and risk specific protein signatures and associated immune cell profiles changes. These findings provide novel biological insights into LCH heterogeneity and identify candidate protein biomarkers associated with disease extent and risk-organ involvement. Further validation in larger independent cohorts is required
candidates.fulltext: 1IntroductionLangerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) is a rare disease characterized by pathological infiltration of CD1a+/CD207+ cells. It exhibits an overall annual incidence of approximately 5 cases per million that predominantly affects children, with an incidence of 4.6 cases per million in individuals under 15 years old and 1 case per million in adults (1). LCH exhibits diverse clinical manifestations and can involve multiple organ systems. The disease is classified into single-system LCH (SS-LCH) and multisystem LCH (MS-LCH) based on the number of involved organs and sites (2). Common sites of LCH involvement include the skin, bones, lungs, liver, and pituitary gland. Among these, the liver, spleen, and bone marrow are defined as high-risk organs (3). Multisystem LCH can be further categorized into high-risk organ involvement [LCH-RO (+)] and no high-risk organ involvement [LCH-RO (–)] based on whether these organs are affected (4). Notably, MS-LCH patients, especially those with high-risk organ involvement, exhibit significantly higher disease-related mortality compared to single-system LCH patients (5, 6). The clinical presentation of LCH is highly heterogeneous, ranging from isolated self-limiting lesions to progressive multi-organ involvement with significant morbidity and mortality. Sequelae may include substantial damage to the endocrine, auditory, skeletal, neurocognitive, pulmonary, and hepatic systems (3, 7).Several prognostic biomarkers have been identified in LCH. At the genetic level, the BRAF gene is currently the only gene with recurrently validated somatic mutations in multiple patients, with the BRAF V600E point mutation detected in approximately 50%-65% of LCH lesions (8, 9). The presence of the BRAF V600E mutation is significantly associated with multisystem LCH involving high-risk organs, disease progression, or recurrence, making it an important genetic biomarker (10–12). Additionally, cytokine levels such as IL-6, IL-10, IL-18, TNF-α, and soluble CD25 (sCD25) have been established as important serological biomarkers for assessing systemic inflammation, disease activity, and prognosis (13–16).The striking histological uniformity of LCH lesions makes it impossible for pathologists to determine whether a biopsy specimen comes from a patient with single-system or multisystem disease, or to assess whether the case represents a moderate-risk or high-risk condition (17). Consequently, the development of additional biomarkers for risk stratification in LCH is both necessary and clinically significant.Through proteomic analysis, this study systematically characterized the molecular features of LCH across different clinical subtypes, including single-system and multisystem disease, as well as risk-organ involvement status. We identified multiple differentially expressed functional modules and candidate protein biomarkers. BICDL2, CD22, CLDN4, DSC3, ELP1, and NOSIP were associated with differences between single-system and multisystem LCH, whereas DOK3, RPL18, and IDI1 were associated with risk-organ involvement. Exploratory machine-learning analyses were further performed to assess whether these candidate proteins contained classification information related to disease extent and risk-organ status. These findings identify candidate protein biomarkers associated with LCH clinical heterogeneity and provide a molecular basis for future validation in independent cohort.2Materials and methods2.1Human sample preparationFormalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue samples used in this study were obtained from surgical resections of pediatric LCH patients at the Guangzhou Women and Children’s Medical Center affiliated with Guangzhou Medical University. All cases were confirmed by pathological diagnosis at the same institution. Diagnosis strictly followed the 2009 International Histiocyte Society guidelines for evaluation and treatment of LCH (18). The study was conducted in accordance with the ethical principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. Clinical data were anonymized to protect patient privacy, and the study protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Guangzhou Women and Children’s Medical Center (Ethics Approval No.: [2025]008A01). The sample groups were as follows: Skin control (n = 10), LCH (n = 56), SS-LCH (n = 25), MS-LCH (n = 31), LCH-RO (−) (n = 17), and LCH-RO (+) (n = 18) (Supplementary Table 1).2.2Micro-proteomic sample preparationFFPE sections of 5 μm thickness were prepared, with 1–2 sections per case. candidates.title: Large-scale plasma proteomics identifies proteins and pathways associated with incident interstitial lung disease.
candidates.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Reliable biomarkers for early interstitial lung disease (ILD) risk stratification are limited; therefore, we aimed to identify prediagnostic proteins associated with incident ILD and develop a long-term prediction model.
METHODS: We analyzed 52,743 UK Biobank participants without baseline ILD and measured 2,923 plasma proteins. Cox models were used to identify proteins associated with incident ILD. Key predictors were selected using LASSO and sequential forward selection within a LightGBM framework. Model performance was assessed using the area under the curve (AUC) and SHAP. Prediagnostic protein trajectories were evaluated using LOESS and clustering. Single-cell transcriptomic data from human idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis lungs were used to explore cellular sources.
RESULTS: During a mean follow-up period of 14.4 years, 814 ILD cases were identified in the cohort. A total of 277 proteins were significantly associated with incident ILD and enriched in immune activation and cytokine signaling pathways. Five proteins (GDF15, LAMP3, SFTPD, EDA2R, and WFDC2) were identified as dominant predictors. Trajectory analysis showed that several ILD-associated proteins deviated from control levels years before diagnosis and could be grouped into four distinct temporal clusters. GDF15, LAMP3, SFTPD, WFDC2, and EGFR showed detectable prediagnostic alterations more than a decade before ILD onset. Furthermore, connective tissue disease (CTD)-ILD displayed a distinct inflammatory proteomic profile, including CXCL13, CCL7, PDCD1, and TNFRSF4. When the five protein biomarkers were combined with clinical variables, the integrated model achieved relatively good predictive accuracy for ILD, with AUCs of 0.938 and 0.908 for 5-year and 10-year ILD risks, respectively. Single-cell analysis indicated that these proteins may predominantly originate from dysregulated alveolar and airway epithelial cells.

candidates.fulltext: IntroductionInterstitial lung disease (ILD) is a heterogeneous group of disorders characterized by progressive lung fibrosis and impaired respiratory function, with significant morbidity and mortality (1). The incidence and prevalence of ILD have markedly increased in recent years. In the United States alone, ILD affects approximately 650,000 individuals and is responsible for an estimated 25,000–30,000 deaths annually (1, 2). Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), the most common and severe form, carries a worse prognosis than many malignancies, with a median survival of 3–5 years from diagnosis (3).While antifibrotic therapies, including nintedanib and pirfenidone, have demonstrated efficacy, their benefits are most pronounced when initiated early, emphasizing the critical need for early detection (4–6). However, the clinical management of ILD remains challenging due to its insidious onset and nonspecific symptoms, which frequently lead to diagnostic delays until a large proportion of patients develop irreversible, end-stage fibrosis (7–9). Current biomarkers for ILD assist in early detection but suffer from low efficacy and an inability to forecast long-term outcomes (10, 11). Pre-symptomatic biomarkers are urgently needed to identify high-risk individuals before structural damage occurs.Recent advances in high-throughput proteomics have revolutionized biomarker discovery for complex diseases (12, 13). However, comprehensive proteomic profiling for ILD risk prediction in large population-based cohorts remains limited. The UK Biobank, with over 500,000 participants, provides rich proteomic data that may help identify molecular biomarkers associated with ILD (14). The availability of longitudinal data coupled with detailed clinical and lifestyle information makes the UK Biobank an invaluable tool for predictive modeling. When proteomics is linked to prospectively ascertained health records, this technology can transform population biobanks into “molecular observatories” capable of charting protein trajectories years before phenotypic expression. Recent exemplars include the identification of NEFL, CSRP3, and MEGF10 as decade-ahead predictors of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and the demonstration that cardiac-specific proteins (NT-proBNP and hs-cTnI) forecast heart failure independent of traditional risk factors (15, 16). Therefore, plasma proteomics may help provide an early warning for ILD, enabling therapeutic intervention at the pre-fibrotic stage and offering a realistic prospect of delaying disease onset.Machine learning algorithms, especially those proficient in high-dimensional data analysis, have shown potential in developing predictive models of disease risk. The Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM) is a gradient-boosting framework ideal for large, high-dimensional datasets, efficiently managing both categorical and continuous variables (17, 18). By capturing intricate relationships and tolerating missing values, its leaf-wise growth boosts both speed and accuracy, excelling in proteomic data rife with complex protein interactions (19, 20). This method may help synthesize various variables, ranging from genetics to environmental and lifestyle factors, and can discern intricate biological signatures from extensive cohorts, thereby predicting an individual’s risk of developing ILD.In this study, we focused on identifying plasma proteins significantly associated with the risk of ILD using the UK Biobank Dataset. In addition, we developed a predictive model based on plasma proteins and clinical variables using the LightGBM method. Shapley Additive explanations (SHAP) were used to evaluate the variables within the machine learning model. Our model identifies the risk factors and proteins associated with incident ILD and identifies patients at a higher risk of developing ILD, offering insights into early intervention and improved disease management.MethodsStudy populationThe UK Biobank is a prospective cohort of 502,357 adults (aged 39–70 years) recruited between 2006 and 2010 through 22 assessment centers embedded within the UK’s National Health Service.Proteomic measurements were only available for a predefined UKB-PPP subset (21, 22). candidates.title: Integrating multi-omics and machine learning to reveal IL1R2-driven macrophage-fibroblast spatial interactions in polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon-induced pulmonary fibrosis.
candidates.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) are ubiquitous environmental toxicants, yet the toxicological mechanisms by which they induce idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) remain poorly understood. This study aims to systematically elucidate the molecular basis and cellular interplay driving PAH-induced pulmonary fibrosis.
METHODS: We first evaluated the toxicological profiles of 16 priority-controlled PAHs using toxicological databases and then conducted in vitro experiments to assess their effects on pulmonary epithelial cells. By integrating transcriptomic data, we combined differential expression analysis, weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA), and Mendelian randomization (MR) to screen IPF-associated genes. Given the well-defined structure of IL1R2, molecular docking and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were employed to evaluate the binding affinity and conformational stability of the 16 PAHs with IL1R2. Finally, using single-cell transcriptomics, we compared the functional disparities between IL1R2-positive and IL1R2-negative macrophages within the fibrotic microenvironment.
RESULTS: In vitro, PAHs exerted cytotoxic effects on pulmonary epithelial cells, manifested primarily as suppressed cell viability, dysregulated inflammatory cytokine expression, and DNA damage. Intersecting the identified IPF-associated genes with PAH-target genes from the CTD database yielded diagnostic and prognostic models, ultimately pinpointing SPP1, IL1R2, and SCGB3A2 as core targets. Molecular docking and MD simulations demonstrated stable binding of the 16 PAHs to IL1R2. Single-cell transcriptomic analysis further revealed that IL1R2-negative macrophages mediate a more pronounced pro-fibrotic phenotype via the IL-1 signaling pathway and exacerbate pro-fibrotic cell-cell communication with fibroblasts.

candidates.fulltext: 1IntroductionPolycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) are a class of organic compounds consisting of two or more fused benzene rings, primarily originating from the incomplete combustion of fossil fuels and biomass (1, 2). As persistent environmental toxicants ubiquitous in the atmosphere, water, and soil, PAHs exhibit high lipid solubility and resistance to degradation. Upon entering the respiratory tract, they readily inflict continuous damage on pulmonary tissues (3, 4).In recent years, the potential association between PAH exposure and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) has garnered increasing attention. IPF is characterized by alveolar epithelial micro-injury and aberrant tissue repair, pathological processes that can be triggered and amplified by the toxic effects of PAHs. Epidemiological studies have demonstrated that elevated levels of urinary PAH metabolites are significantly associated with a substantial decline in lung function (5), highlighting the destructive impact of PAH exposure on the lung parenchyma. Mechanistically, upon entering the alveolar space, PAHs not only directly compromise the alveolar epithelial barrier but also disrupt the local immune microenvironment. Low-molecular-weight PAHs (e.g., phenanthrene and fluorene) can induce profound oxidative stress and inflammatory responses in human bronchial epithelial cells (6, 7). Such toxicant-induced epithelial injury and oxidative imbalance represent key initiating events in the pathogenesis of IPF. Furthermore, PAHs can mediate the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines and the aberrant activation of macrophages (8–10), thereby further driving aberrant tissue remodeling. In contrast, high-molecular-weight PAHs (e.g., benzo[a]pyrene) exhibit stronger lipophilicity, allowing them to persist longer within pulmonary tissues. Their reactive metabolites (e.g., diol epoxides) can bind to DNA to form adducts, leading to cellular mutations and interfering with normal cellular metabolism and gene expression (11, 12), consequently exacerbating chronic pathological damage in the lung. Notably, the impact of PAHs on pulmonary health can be traced back to early developmental stages. Studies indicate that maternal exposure to PAHs can exacerbate hyperoxia-induced lung injury in neonates (13). Such early-life exposure may alter pulmonary developmental programming, thereby increasing an individual’s subsequent susceptibility to toxicant-induced fibrosis.Given the inherent limitations of relying solely on network toxicology predictions to construct complex pathogenic networks, this study integrates multi-omics analyses, computational chemistry simulations, and in vitro cellular assays to systematically elucidate the toxicological mechanisms underlying PAH-induced IPF. Initially, we evaluated the cytotoxicity and DNA damage potential of 16 priority-controlled PAHs. Subsequently, by integrating weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) and Mendelian randomization (MR), we screened IPF-associated genes and intersected them with PAH toxicological targets from the CTD database to construct diagnostic and prognostic models. This pipeline ultimately pinpointed SPP1, IL1R2, and SCGB3A2 as core targets. Focusing on IL1R2, molecular docking and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were employed to verify the conformational stability and high binding affinity of PAHs to this receptor. Finally, leveraging single-cell and spatial transcriptomic data, we revealed the functional remodeling of IL1R2-negative macrophages within the fibrotic microenvironment and characterized their spatial intercellular communication network with fibroblasts. This study aims to clarify the molecular basis and cellular interplay driving PAH-induced pulmonary toxicity, thereby providing multidimensional scientific evidence for the risk assessment and clinical intervention of environmental pollutant-related pulmonary fibrosis.2Materials and methods2.1Toxicity prediction and analysis of PAHsTo systematically assess the toxicological profiles of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), we retrieved the structural data of 16 representative PAHs from the PubChem database and predicted their toxicity using the ADMETlab 3.0 platform (14). The selected target compounds included naphthalene, acenaphthylene, acenaphthene, fluorene, phenanthrene, anthracene, fluoranthene, pyrene, benz[a]anthracene, chrysene, benzo[b]fluoranthene, benzo[k]fluoranthene, benzo[a]pyrene, indeno[1,2,3-cd]pyrene, dibenz[a,h]anthracene, and benzo[ghi]perylene. candidates.title: Discovering Biomarkers for Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis by Correlating Serum Extracellular Vesicle Proteins With Clinical Data.
candidates.abstract: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a chronic and progressive disease with a poor prognosis due to the irreversible loss of lung structure. Unfortunately, distinguishing between this condition and other interstitial pneumonias (IPs) is quite difficult. Hence, we herein present a machine learning method to identify IPF biomarkers by correlating serum extracellular vesicle proteomic data with clinical data for 507 patients with IPs and 39 healthy control subjects. We applied multi-class sparse correlation analysis to detecting proteins associated with each disease-specific IP phenotype, and identified surfactant protein B (SFTPB) and BPI fold containing family B member 1 (BPIFB1) as potential IPF biomarker candidates for discriminating IPF from other IPs, with area under the receiver operating characteristic curve scores of 0.679 and 0.678, respectively, outperforming existing biomarkers for IPF. Combinations of SFTPB and BPIFB1 achieved better discriminative performance over the use of SFTPB or BPIFB1 individually. The identified biomarker candidates can be expected to facilitate the noninvasive diagnosis of IPF.

candidates.title: CXCL12: a key gene in IPF-COPD pathogenesis and its therapeutic potential.
candidates.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Shared core genes and molecular mechanisms relevant to the pathological overlap between idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) were investigated to inform future diagnostic and therapeutic research.
METHODS: Gene expression profiles were analysed using differential expression gene (DEG) analysis, weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA), and functional enrichment. A random forest (RF) model incorporating a multi-feature selection mechanism was used to identify core genes in IPF patients with COPD. The expression levels, diagnostic performance, and immune cell relationships of these genes were analysed, and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) was used to assess the expression patterns of the core genes. Finally, drug predictions were made based on the core genes. Molecular docking and 100-ns molecular dynamics simulations were further performed to evaluate candidate CXCL12-ligand interactions, and CXCL12 expression was experimentally validated in BEAS-2B cells after cigarette smoke extract, bleomycin, and combined stimulation.
RESULTS: CXCL12 was identified as a core gene for IPF combined with COPD. This gene exhibited high expression levels in the dataset, with receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve area under the curve (AUC) values of 0.78, 0.67, 1.00, and 0.86, respectively. Exploratory analysis of CIBERSORT-estimated immune-cell proportions showed significant differences in CD8+ T cells and resting memory CD4+ T cells between the CXCL12-high and CXCL12-low groups. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) indicates that CXCL12 exhibits significantly increased expression in endothelial cells of COPD and fibroblast cells of IPF, providing valuable insights into the molecular mechanisms. candidates.fulltext: IntroductionChronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) are both respiratory diseases associated with high mortality worldwide. According to recent Global Burden of Disease estimates, COPD remains the third leading cause of death globally [1–3]. IPF is the most common and fatal form of idiopathic interstitial pneumonia, with a median survival of only 3 to 5 years after diagnosis [4, 5]. Although COPD and IPF have traditionally been regarded as mutually exclusive in terms of pathology, imaging features, and patterns of airflow limitation, observations made more than half a century ago had already suggested that the two conditions can coexist in the same patient [6]. In 2005, Cottin et al. first proposed the concept of “combined pulmonary fibrosis and emphysema” (CPFE), which has since been progressively recognised as a distinct clinical entity [7]. COPD and IPF share several epidemiological and exposure-related risk factors, including smoking, ageing, and occupational or environmental inhalational exposures [8, 9]. In this context, Lee S.H. et al. analysed 1,546 patients with IPF in 2019 and reported that IPF may coexist with COPD, with a coexistence rate of approximately 9.2% [10]. In 2023, a nationwide cohort study by Lee J.H. et al. indicated that COPD had become the most prevalent respiratory comorbidity among patients with IPF, accounting for approximately 37% of cases [11]. To date, multiple international guidelines and systematic reviews have indicated that IPF frequently coexists with other respiratory diseases [8, 12–16]. Among these, emphysema and COPD represent common pulmonary comorbidities in patients with IPF. Their co-occurrence can complicate radiological interpretation, pulmonary function assessment, and treatment decision-making, underscoring the need to recognise and manage these overlapping conditions throughout the diagnostic and therapeutic process.From a pathophysiological perspective, COPD-induced chronic airway inflammation may accelerate injury to the alveolar epithelium and interstitium, thereby promoting fibrotic development [17]. Conversely, fibrotic remodelling reduces lung tissue compliance, resulting in impaired ventilation and hypoxia. These changes may further amplify inflammatory responses and interfere with tissue repair, thereby promoting a self-reinforcing cycle of emphysematous destruction, fibrosis, and chronic inflammation. Clinically, the major symptoms of CPFE, COPD, and IPF include chronic cough and progressive dyspnoea. In COPD, chronic cough and sputum production may persist for years before airflow limitation becomes apparent, and the disease is often overlooked because of its slow progression [18]. In IPF, dyspnoea and cough represent the dominant symptom burden, with dyspnoea affecting more than 90% of patients and chronic cough affecting up to 80% of patients, sometimes even preceding diagnosis [19, 20]. Overall, symptoms in patients with CPFE more closely resemble those of IPF and are primarily characterised by dyspnoea and a pronounced dry cough, whereas sputum production is atypical. At present, evidence regarding CPFE treatment remains limited. General measures, such as smoking cessation and avoidance of environmental exposures, may slow disease progression [21]. Although inhaled bronchodilators with or without corticosteroids may benefit patients with CPFE who exhibit marked airflow limitation, the supporting evidence remains limited, and further investigation is warranted [22].At the molecular and cellular levels, an increasing body of research indicates that COPD and IPF share several pathogenic factors and pathways, including chronic smoking exposure, ageing-related mechanisms, oxidative stress, epithelial injury, and abnormal repair processes [23, 24]. These factors have been reported to play important roles in the development and progression of both diseases. At the same time, COPD and IPF differ markedly in their central pathological axes. COPD is primarily characterised by small airway remodelling and emphysema resulting from chronic bronchitis, basal cell destruction, and loss of elastic tissue. By contrast, IPF is mainly characterised by abnormal epithelial-mesenchymal interactions following epithelial injury, activation of fibroblasts and myofibroblasts, and excessive extracellular matrix deposition within the pulmonary interstitium [25, 26]. Existing GWAS and genetic studies have demonstrated that shared risk genes for IPF and COPD include FAM13A, DSP, and TERT [27]. candidates.title: Influenza-associated acute respiratory deterioration fulfilling acute exacerbation criteria in hospitalized patients with interstitial lung disease: a single-center retrospective cohort study.
candidates.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Acute exacerbation (AE) of interstitial lung disease (ILD) is life threatening, but data on acute respiratory deterioration fulfilling AE criteria after laboratory-confirmed influenza infection are limited. The current study investigated the incidence, clinical features, and outcomes of such events after laboratory-confirmed influenza in hospitalized patients with ILD.
METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed adults with pre-existing ILD who were hospitalized with influenza at Toranomon Hospital between April 2014 and April 2019. Influenza was confirmed by rapid diagnostic tests. Fulfillment of the AE criteria was confirmed by two pulmonologists and one radiologist. Baseline characteristics and outcomes were compared between patients with and without AE-criteria events. The Mann-Whitney U test or Fisher's exact test were used for between-group comparisons, and the Kaplan-Meier method and the log-rank test were used for survival analysis.
RESULTS: Of 927 patients hospitalized with ILD during the study period, 47 had laboratory-confirmed influenza, and 10 of these patients (21.3%) developed AE-criteria events. The median interval from influenza diagnosis to event onset was 5.0 days. Compared with patients without AE-criteria events, those with AE-criteria events had lower percent predicted forced vital capacity (70.0% versus 88.0%, p = 0.041) and higher ILD-GAP stage. The in-hospital mortality rate in patients with AE-criteria events was 30.0%. Overall survival from influenza diagnosis appeared shorter in patients with AE-criteria events in unadjusted analysis.
CONCLUSIONS: Acute respiratory deterioration fulfilling AE criteria occurred in approximately one fifth of hospitalized patients with ILD after laboratory-confirmed influenza and was associated with high in-hospital mortality. Unadjusted analysis also suggested shorter overall survival in these patients. These findings should be considered exploratory and hypothesis-generating, and require confirmation
candidates.fulltext: BackgroundInterstitial lung disease (ILD) encompasses a heterogeneous group of diffuse parenchymal lung diseases, all characterized by varying degrees of inflammation and fibrosis within the lung interstitium. It can be classified as idiopathic interstitial pneumonia (IIP) or secondary forms associated with specific conditions such as connective tissue disease (CTD), hypersensitivity pneumonitis (HP), drug-induced lung injury, and occupational exposure.Acute exacerbation (AE) of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is defined by the revised criteria proposed by the International Working Group report [1] as follows: “Cases which show sudden worsening of respiratory symptoms within one month, with new bilateral ground-glass opacities, or consolidation on high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT), in which cardiac failure or fluid overload are excluded as the primary cause”. AE of IPF has a poor prognosis, with in-hospital mortality rates of approximately 30%–50%.Patients with chronic lung diseases, including ILD, are particularly vulnerable to severe complications owing to their reduced pulmonary reserve. Viral infections have been implicated as potential triggers of AE [2]. AE triggered by seasonal influenza infection is occasionally encountered in daily clinical practice. However, evidence regarding this phenomenon is limited, with research primarily confined to isolated case reports describing such associations [3]. Current clinical practice guidelines recommend performing annual influenza vaccination in patients with IPF to reduce the risk of AE; however, data directly linking vaccination to reduced AE risk remains limited [4, 5].The aim of the current study was to investigate the incidence, clinical features, and outcomes of acute respiratory deterioration fulfilling AE criteria in hospitalized patients with ILD following laboratory-confirmed influenza infection. We also compared baseline clinical characteristics between patients with and without AE-criteria events.MethodsStudy participantsThe study enrolled eligible patients admitted to Toranomon Hospital between April 2014 and April 2019. The inclusion criteria were adults (≥ 18 years) with a pre-existing diagnosis of ILD and radiologic and/or histopathologic evidence of chronic fibrosis. ILD was defined based on clinical, radiological, and/or histopathological findings, as documented in medical records. Diagnoses included IPF, IIP other than IPF, CTD-ILD, drug-induced ILD, and fibrotic HP. Influenza infection was diagnosed using the ESPLINE Influenza A&B-N rapid influenza diagnostic test (Fujirebio Inc., Tokyo, Japan) performed on nasopharyngeal swab specimens.Study designThis single-center, retrospective cohort study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the institutional ethics committee of Toranomon Hospital (approval number 1961). Patients were classified into the AE-criteria event group or non-event group based on whether they developed acute respiratory deterioration fulfilling AE criteria within 1 month of influenza diagnosis. AE criteria were based on those proposed by Collard et al. [1], requiring acute worsening of dyspnea within 1 month, new bilateral ground-glass opacities and/or consolidation on HRCT, and exclusion of heart failure or fluid overload as the primary cause. Under the revised AE framework, infection was not considered an exclusion criterion. Therefore, events were classified based on fulfillment of the AE criteria rather than being attributed definitively to influenza-triggered AE-ILD. In the patients with AE-criteria events, fulfillment of the AE criteria was confirmed by two pulmonologists and one radiologist.Data collection and outcomesVariables recorded at the time of influenza diagnosis and hospitalization included age, sex, body mass index (BMI), smoking history, comorbidities, vital signs, arterial blood gas values, and serum biomarkers (including Krebs von den Lungen-6 [KL-6], surfactant protein D [SP-D], and surfactant protein A [SP-A]). Pulmonary function test results (vital capacity [VC], percent predicted VC [%VC], forced vital capacity [FVC], percent predicted FVC [%FVC], carbon monoxide diffusion capacity [DLco], and percent predicted DLco [%DLco]), and the 6-minute walk test results were obtained from the most recent assessments performed within 1 year before influenza diagnosis.Treatment-related variables included antifibrotic or corticosteroid use, seasonal influenza vaccination status (including timing within the same season), influenza virus type, and antiviral therapy (oseltamivir, peramivir, baloxavir, or laninamivir). Information on polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing for influenza and other respiratory viruses was extracted from the medical records. candidates.title: Umbilical cord blood mononuclear cells for inflammation-related diseases: a narrative review of immunomodulatory mechanisms, clinical evidence, and translational perspectives.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Dysregulated inflammation contributes to both acute organ injury and chronic degenerative disease. Umbilical cord blood mononuclear cells (UCB-MNCs) constitute a heterogeneous cord-blood-derived cell product characterized by relative immune immaturity, potentially lower alloreactivity, and a higher proportion of naïve regulatory T-cell phenotypes than adult peripheral blood. UCB-MNCs have therefore been investigated as a candidate immunomodulatory cell therapy, but a critical cross-organ synthesis of their proposed mechanisms and clinical evidence remains limited. This narrative review critically integrates preclinical and clinical evidence on UCB-MNCs across neurological, cardiovascular, hepatic, renal, and pulmonary inflammation-related diseases. The clinical literature comprised 29 published reports involving approximately 1358 participants, of whom about 944 received UCB-MNC-containing interventions. These reports suggest generally acceptable short-term tolerability, but clinical efficacy remains uncertain because most studies were small, uncontrolled, methodologically limited, and clinically heterogeneous. Across preclinical studies, the most recurrent findings were predominantly associative and included immune-state-related marker changes, context-dependent adaptive immune regulation, and selective cytokine-network remodeling. Single-study perturbation or rescue experiments provided Grade B support for contributory IL-22-STAT3 signaling in acute liver injury, Nrf2-dependent autophagy and mitochondrial protection in septic acute kidney injury, Hedgehog-associated neurogenesis in neonatal brain injury, and CD40/CD40L-dependent amyloid-β clearance. Grade C evidence was limited to single-report associations involving neurotrophic factors, blood-brain barrier-related readouts, renal antifibrotic changes, and bronchopulmonary-dysplasia-associated alveolar-vascular remodeling. candidates.fulltext: BackgroundAs a core component of biological defense, the systematic study of inflammation can be traced back to the four classical cardinal signs—redness, swelling, heat, and pain—described by the ancient Roman physician Cornelius Celsus. Rudolph Virchow later introduced dysfunction as a fifth cardinal sign, highlighting the functional impairment that may accompany inflammatory processes [1]. The modern conceptual framework of inflammation comprises four core components: inducers, including pathogen-associated molecular patterns and damage-associated molecular patterns; sensors, such as pattern-recognition receptors; mediators, including cytokines; and effectors, particularly immune and endothelial cell systems. The spatial and temporal interactions among these components determine the biological characteristics and consequences of different inflammatory responses [1, 2].Successful acute inflammation can eliminate pathogens and limit the spread of damage, and through the promotion of resolving mediators, actively terminate the inflammatory response, transitioning to the repair phase. Therefore, controlled acute inflammation is beneficial, but dysregulated acute inflammation can be fatal [2, 3]. When acute inflammation does not completely subside, or when there is an autoimmune response or tissue homeostasis imbalance, it can lead to a prolonged, low-intensity chronic inflammatory state [4]. Notably, when tissues are subjected to non-infectious stressors (such as hypoxia, metabolic abnormalities, heat stress, etc.) or are in a state of dysfunction, resident macrophages or mast cells can mediate a chronic, low-grade, asymptomatic systemic inflammation between tissue homeostasis and classical inflammation, known as para-inflammation. This is an adaptive response that plays an essential role in maintaining tissue homeostasis; however, when this adaptive response is excessive, the body’s stable set point shifts and evolves into dysregulated para-inflammation. Chronic low-grade inflammation characterizes various chronic diseases, such as obesity, type 2 diabetes, atherosclerosis, asthma, and neurodegenerative diseases [2].In conclusion, inflammation is a complex process involving various molecules, cells, and signaling pathways, and is associated with nearly all diseases [5]. The central issue lies in the uncontrolled degree of the inflammatory response. Therefore, how to regulate the “degree” of inflammation and achieve an effective transition from damage to repair has become an important challenge in the treatment of inflammation-related diseases (Fig. 1).Fig. 1The inflammation pathway and divergent outcomes of infection-induced, tissue injury-induced, and stress-induced inflammatory responses. The top panel illustrates the general inflammation pathway: inducers (PAMPs/DAMPs) activate sensors (PRRs), triggering mediators (cytokines/chemokines) that act on effectors (immune cells/tissues/organs). The left column shows infection-induced acute inflammation (hours to days), which may undergo controlled resolution restoring homeostasis, excessive response causing cytokine storm and acute severe diseases (sepsis, MODS), or incomplete resolution progressing to chronic inflammation. The middle column depicts tissue injury-induced inflammation (days to weeks), resulting in either successful repair via IL-1α/IL-33-mediated regeneration or failed repair leading to fibrosis, metaplasia, or tumor. The right column illustrates stress-induced para-inflammation, a low-grade adaptive state driven by non-infectious stressors, which either maintains homeostasis or transitions maladaptively to chronic diseases (atherosclerosis, type 2 diabetes, neurodegeneration, obesity). Dashed arrows indicate cross-pathway interactions between inflammatory types. Abbreviations: PAMPs, pathogen-associated molecular patterns; DAMPs, damage-associated molecular patterns; PRRs, pattern recognition receptors; SPMs, specialized pro-resolving mediators; MODS, multiple organ dysfunction syndrome. candidates.fulltext: BackgroundAnti-synthetase syndrome (ASyS) encompasses a heterogeneous spectrum of inflammatory myopathies characterized by the presence of anti-aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase antibodies and a multitude of clinical manifestations including myositis, interstitial lung disease (ILD), arthritis, mechanic’s hands, Raynaud’s phenomenon, fever, and systemic inflammation [1, 2]. ILD, which develops in the majority of patients, is the most challenging to manage and represents the leading cause of morbidity and mortality [2, 3]. Its severity ranges from fulminant disease with acute respiratory failure to chronic but progressive fibrosis [4, 5]. There is no standardized treatment for ASyS-ILD, largely because no randomized controlled trials have compared agents in this disease [6]. In practice, management relies on moderate-to-high-dose glucocorticoids combined with conventional immunosuppressants such as cyclophosphamide, mycophenolate, or azathioprine [7]. Even so, about a third of patients keep progressing on this regimen and require rescue therapy, for which rituximab and Janus kinase inhibition have shown promise, though only in observational studies [8, 9]. Such difficult-to-treat disease usually takes the form of glucocorticoid resistance, glucocorticoid dependence with cumulative toxicity [10], or progressive pulmonary fibrosis (PPF), in which fibrosis advances irreversibly despite immunomodulation [5]. For the fibrotic phenotype, an antifibrotic such as nintedanib may be considered to slow the decline in lung function; [11] its benefit in ASyS-ILD specifically, however, has not been confirmed in controlled trials and rests largely on extrapolation from broader cohorts of PPF and small retrospective series [12]. No established strategy reliably controls these refractory phenotypes, which therefore remain a critical unmet clinical need.Interleukin-6 (IL-6) has emerged as an attractive therapeutic target for ASyS based on accumulating mechanistic and clinical rationale. In experimental myositis models, IL-6 deficiency attenuates disease severity [13], and serum IL-6 correlates with clinical disease activity and appears to operate at the inflammation-fibrosis interface in ILD pathogenesis [14]. This raises the possibility that its blockade could simultaneously control active inflammation and modulate fibrotic progression. Tocilizumab, a humanised anti-IL-6 receptor monoclonal antibody, has already shown efficacy in stabilising lung function in systemic sclerosis-ILD [15] and rheumatoid arthritis-associated ILD [16], providing a biological rationale for its use in ASyS. Clinical evidence in this specific context, however, remains confined to scattered case reports [17–22], with no systematic evaluation to date.To address this gap, we conducted a real-world evaluation of tocilizumab in refractory ASyS-ILD, stratifying patients by the three phenotypes defined above, with the aim of characterising clinical responsiveness to IL-6 blockade across distinct disease contexts.MethodsStudy design and populationThis retrospective cohort study enrolled consecutive patients with refractory ASyS-ILD who initiated tocilizumab at the China-Japan Friendship Hospital between October 2023 and July 2025 and completed at least 3 months of treatment. The study was approved by the Institutional Ethics Committee of China-Japan Friendship Hospital (Approval number: 2022-KY-156) and conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants.Eligible patients were aged ≥ 18 years, met the ASyS diagnostic criteria of Solomon et al. [23], had ILD confirmed on high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT), fulfilled the definition of refractory ASyS-ILD (see below), and had complete baseline and follow-up data available. candidates.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Respirable dust and fibres in occupational settings are major contributors to lung dysfunction, imposing a significant societal burden. Following the ban on asbestos in most countries, silica and coal mine dust have emerged as primary concerns due to their abundance and persistence in workplace dust. Exposure to dust containing these elements has been strongly linked to pulmonary fibrosis and lung cancer.
MAIN BODY: Extensive research has explored the molecular mechanisms underlying respirable occupational dust-induced cytotoxicity and immune dysregulation. The toxic effects of respirable occupational dust and fibres are largely induced by oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, lysosomal damage, inflammasome activation and immune suppression. These exposures can trigger multiple cell death pathways, including ferroptosis, necrosis, and pyroptosis. While sharing common toxicological features, silica, coal dust, and asbestos exhibit distinct toxic effects on various pulmonary cell types involved in fibrosis and cancer progression. The immunological consequences of dust exposure are profound, as dust-induced activation of macrophages and neutrophils, together with natural killer (NK) cell dysfunction, sustains chronic inflammation and disrupts epithelial repair and fibroblast regulation, thereby promoting fibrosis and tumorigenesis. Although no curative treatments exist for pulmonary fibrosis, especially coal workers' pneumoconiosis and silicosis, this review also discusses emerging therapeutic approaches, such as antifibrotic agents and immunotherapy, aimed at mitigating lung fibrosis and lung cancer.
CONCLUSION: This review summarises recent findings on the toxicological mechanisms underlying respirable occupational dust- and fibre-induced lung diseases, with a focus on crystalline silica, and coal dust and asbestos, especially those bearing reduced iron minerals.
